sentences.text: Enchodus species ranged from small to medium sizes, with the largest species, E. zinensis, reaching 172.2 cm in length.
E. petrosus typically measured around 76.7 cm but could exceed 1 meter, and its fossils are common in formations like the Niobrara Chalk and Pierre Shale within the Western Interior Seaway.
Some Enchodus species, like E. parvus, were very small, measuring only a few inches in length.
Enchodus remains are frequently found in the stomach contents of larger predators such as sharks, mosasaurs, plesiosaurs, and the seabird Baptornis advenus.
Large specimens of E. petrosus possessed fangs longer than 6 cm (2.4 inches).
The genus Enchodus was first described by Louis Agassiz in 1835.

In 2026, Nelson, Murray, and Brinkman described fossil material of E. petrosus and E. cf. gladiolus from the Upper Cretaceous Bearpaw Formation in Alberta, Canada, including the largest articulated skull of the genus reported to date.
Enchodus was a predatory species, indicated by its large fangs, sleek body, and large eyes.
Large E. petrosus individuals had fangs over 6 cm long, giving their skulls a resemblance to modern deep-sea fishes like anglerfish and viperfish.
Enchodus species are generally classified into two clades: North American and Mediterranean.
Enchodus belongs to the family Enchodontidae.
Enchodus fossils range from the Albian to the Maastrichtian stages, with possible records from the Barremian and Paleogene.
Enchodus fossils have been discovered worldwide.
The earliest known Enchodus species is E. zimapanensis, found in the late Albian-aged El Doctor Formation of Mexico.
Potentially earlier Enchodus remains from the late Barremian/early Aptian of Brazil exist, but they are too fragmentary to be confidently assigned to the genus.
The potentially latest Enchodus remains are from the earliest Eocene of Barmer, India.
It is debated whether post-Cretaceous Enchodus records represent actual survival or are merely reworked Cretaceous material.
